goals: Match common distributions to real processes
Use binomial and Poisson for counts
Know where the t and chi-square distributions appear
why: Choosing the right distribution is choosing the right model of reality: call-centre staffing (Poisson), defect rates (binomial), waiting times (exponential). The wrong choice gives wrong risk estimates.
explain: **Binomial**: the number of successes in n yes/no trials with success probability p. Example: how many of 20 leads close when each closes with p = 0.1.
**Poisson**: the number of events in a fixed interval when events happen independently at an average rate λ. Example: calls per minute, defects per metre of cable.
**Exponential**: the waiting time between Poisson events. Example: minutes until the next customer arrives.

**Uniform**: every value in a range is equally likely. **t-distribution**: like the normal but with fatter tails, used when estimating a mean from a small sample. **Chi-square**: the distribution of sums of squared normals, used in tests on counts and variances.

example.title: Binomial: how lucky is a good week in sales?
steps: A salesperson closes 10% of leads and has 20 leads this week: fixed tries, yes/no, same p → Binomial(n = 20, p = 0.1)
P(0 deals) = 0.9²⁰ = 0.1216 → about one week in eight she closes nothing, purely by chance
example.result: An average performer has a "great week" of 4+ deals about 13% of the time and a zero week about 12% of the time. Judging people on one week mostly rewards and punishes luck.

mistakes: Modelling counts with a normal distribution when counts are small.
Using Poisson when the variance is much larger than the mean (over-dispersion). Try negative binomial instead.
takeaways: Poisson = events per interval; exponential = time between them
t for small-sample means; chi-square for counts

practice.code:
from scipy.stats import binom, poisson
print(binom.pmf(0, 20, 0.1).round(4), binom.pmf(2, 20, 0.1).round(4))  # 0.1216 0.2852
print((1 - binom.cdf(3, 20, 0.1)).round(4))                           # 0.133  P(4+ deals)
print(poisson.pmf(0, 3).round(4), poisson.sf(6, 3).round(4))           # 0.0498 0.0335  calls, λ = 3/min

check.why: A count of independent events per interval.
